title: Home & everyday objects
goal: Describe your home, say where things are (in, on, under, near) and say what there is and isn't.
intro: Tamil expresses location with **suffixes** and **postpositions** that follow the noun: 'in the house' is வீட்டுல *vīṭṭula* (house-in), 'on the table' is மேசை மேல *mēsai mēla* (table on). And 'there is / there isn't' is just **இருக்கு / இல்ல**.

vocab.note: oblique: வீட்டு- vīṭṭu- (வீட்டுல 'at home', வீட்டுக்கு 'to home')

phrases.en: The bag is under the bed.
How many rooms are there in your house?
There are two bedrooms in our house.

grammar.title: 'In / at': the locative -ல (written -இல்)
grammar.body:
To say **in** or **at** a place, add **-ல** *-la* in speech (written **-இல்** *-il*). After a vowel a glide -ய- or -வ- appears: சென்னை → சென்னையில *Chennaiyila*.

Many nouns have a special **oblique** stem before suffixes:
• words ending in -டு / -று double the consonant: வீடு → வீட்டுல *vīṭṭula*, ஆறு → ஆத்துல *āttula* (in the river)
• words ending in -ம் change it to -த்து: மரம் → மரத்துல *marattula*
• after most other consonants -ல is added directly: ஆஃபீஸ் → ஆஃபீஸ்ல, பஸ் → பஸ்ல (but கண் → கண்ணுல, with -உ-)

The same oblique stem is used before -க்கு (to), -ஓட (of) and other suffixes.

examples.en: The pot is in the kitchen.
The book is in the bag.
The bird is in the tree.

grammar.title: Postpositions: on, under, near, in front, behind
grammar.body:
Other positions are expressed by **postpositions** placed **after** the noun. In speech they usually follow the bare noun (or the oblique stem):

X மேல *mēla* — on / above X
X கீழ *kīḻa* — under X
X உள்ள *uḷḷa* — inside X
X வெளிய *veḷiya* — outside X
X பக்கத்துல *pakkattula* — near / next to X
X முன்னாடி *munnāḍi* — in front of X
X பின்னாடி *pinnāḍi* — behind X
X-க்கும் Y-க்கும் நடுவுல — between X and Y

With pronouns, use the oblique: என் பக்கத்துல 'next to me', அதுக்கு மேல 'on top of it'.

examples.en: The TV is on the wall.
The cat is under the chair.
There's a tree in front of the house.
Our house is between the temple and the shop.

grammar.title: There is / there isn't: இருக்கு and இல்ல
grammar.body:
**இருக்கு** *irukku* (written இருக்கிறது) means both 'it is (located)' and 'there is / there are'. Its negative is simply **இல்ல** *illa* (written இல்லை), which works for every person and number: 'I'm not there', 'there are no rooms', 'he isn't home'.

For people, the verb agrees: அவரு இருக்காரு 'he is there'; but the negative stays இல்ல: அவரு இல்ல 'he isn't there'.

examples.en: There's no window in the room.

dialogue.title: Looking at a flat
dialogue.setting: Sarah is shown a flat to rent by the owner, Mr Kumar.

lines.speaker: Kumar
lines.en: Come, come in. This is the living room.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: It's nice. How many bedrooms are there?

lines.speaker: Kumar
lines.en: Two. One here, the other upstairs.

lines.speaker: Kumar
lines.en: Behind the living room. The bathroom is next to it.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: Is there a fan in the bedroom?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: Is there a bed, table, everything?

lines.speaker: Kumar
lines.en: There's a bed but no table.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: OK. When will you give me the key?

culture: Shoes and sandals are taken off before entering a Tamil home (and always before temples). Many homes have a kōlam (கோலம்) — a pattern drawn in rice flour at the threshold each morning. The 'hall' is the usual word for the main living room, and most houses have a pūjai corner or room (பூஜை அறை) for worship.
